transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I’m here because everybody keeps telling me I’m making too much of it, like I don’t know my own house. But I know what’s been going on. My wife’s relative—he came into the house to get at me. That’s what this is.

My tools don’t just move by themselves, you know? I keep them where I keep them. I’ve worked with my hands my whole life, and I know when something’s been touched. And then the fishing—every weekend, it’s something, plans spoiled, things not where they’re supposed to be. People act like that’s all coincidence, but after months of it, you start seeing it plain.

He’s trying to take over my place. Push me out. And somehow I’m the one sitting here having to explain it.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear, or seen things that others didn't see, during this time?

I don’t know… I mean, I’m not sitting there seeing ghosts or hearing some big booming voice, if that’s what you mean. It’s more like—look, when you’ve lived in a place long enough, you know the sounds it makes. Pipes, floorboards, garage door settling. I can tell the difference.

But people make it sound like I’m inventing things. I’m not. My bench was set up a certain way, and then it wasn’t. Same with my tackle box—had that thing since before my son was in middle school, and I know where every little lure goes. So no, I don’t think it’s about “seeing things.” It’s about somebody being in my space and everyone acting like I’m supposed to ignore it.
Have you been using any recreational drugs, alcohol, or other substances recently, particularly in the months since these suspicions started?

I mean… no, not like that. I’m not out partying or doing whatever people think. I go to work, I come home, I try to keep my things in order. That’s it.

I’ve had a beer here and there like anybody, but this isn’t because of that. My uncle used to drink too much—different story entirely, ruined every holiday for a while—and people always want to blame the easiest thing. But I know when something’s off in my own garage. That doesn’t come from a bottle.

Can you tell me exactly how many months ago you first started noticing these things—like the tools being moved or the fishing trips being spoiled—and has this belief that your wife's relative is trying to push you out been constant since then, without any breaks?

About nine months, I’d say. It started after he moved into our home—my wife’s relative. That’s when I began noticing the tools weren’t right, things shifted around, and then the fishing weekends started getting messed with.

And yes, it’s been… I mean, it hasn’t gone away. Once you see the pattern, you can’t unsee it. People want to make it sound like I woke up one day and decided this, but nine months is a long time to watch someone edge their way into your house. I remember because around then I was working that early shift, and I’d come home tired, and I’d still notice if my stuff had been moved—because that’s my space, you know?
Have you had any recent head injuries, seizures, or been diagnosed with any other medical or neurological conditions around the time these suspicions started?

I don’t… I don’t know what you mean by “neurological” exactly. I mean, I haven’t had some big thing happen, if that’s what you’re asking. No ambulance, no waking up on the floor with people standing over me.

I hit my head plenty over the years at work, you know, bumping into racks or crawling under something when we’re assembling parts, but that’s just work. Guys joke about needing hard hats even in the break room sometimes. But around when all this started? I can’t think of anything special like that.

And I haven’t been told anything like… seizures or whatever. Nobody’s sat me down and said that. This started because things in the house changed, not because I had some medical episode.

The circumscribed, non-bizarre nature of the delusion, absence of hallucinations or thought disorder, and duration >1 month support delusional disorder over schizophrenia or unspecified psychosis.
